name: Citalopram (Celexa)
summary: SSRI antidepressant used for depression and anxiety-related conditions. Takes 1–2 weeks to start helping mood, with full effects in 4–6 weeks. Higher doses can affect heart rhythm (QT prolongation).
description: Citalopram (Celexa) is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) used to treat depression and several anxiety-related conditions. It works by boosting serotonin, a brain chemical that helps regulate mood and worry. Most people take it once a day. It does not work immediately—improvement usually builds slowly over weeks. High doses can affect the heart's electrical rhythm, so there are strict maximum dose limits, especially for adults over 60 or people with heart conditions.
patient_summary: Citalopram (Celexa) is an antidepressant that helps with low mood, anxiety, and related symptoms by increasing serotonin in the brain. You usually take it once a day. It doesn’t work right away—most people start to feel some improvement after 1–2 weeks, with full benefit in about 4–6 weeks. Common side effects include nausea, tiredness, dry mouth, and changes in sleep or sexual function. At higher doses it can affect heart rhythm, so your doctor may limit the dose and sometimes order an EKG (heart tracing). Never stop suddenly without talking to your prescriber.

linked_conditions.context: FDA-approved for major depressive disorder in adults. Considered a first-line SSRI for many patients.
Commonly used off-label for generalized anxiety disorder. Start low (10 mg daily) and increase slowly to reduce initial jitteriness.
Used off-label for panic disorder. Often started at 10 mg to minimize early activation, then titrated to 20–40 mg.
Used off-label for social anxiety disorder. May require 4–6 weeks at a therapeutic dose before judging response.
Alternative off-label option for OCD. Often requires higher doses, but citalopram is less favored due to dose-related QT prolongation.
Sometimes used off-label for PTSD when other SSRIs or SNRIs are not tolerated or ineffective.
Can be used continuously or only during the luteal phase or at symptom onset for PMDD.
Alternative off-label option for hot flashes in menopause when hormone therapy is not appropriate.
Sometimes used off-label to reduce binge episodes, though not first-line.
Used off-label for agitation and aggression in dementia at lower doses with careful monitoring, especially in adults over 60.

contraindications: Known allergy or serious reaction to citalopram or any of its ingredients
Current or recent (within 14 days) use of an MAOI for psychiatric conditions
Concurrent use with pimozide (dangerous heart rhythm changes)
Known congenital long QT syndrome or prior serious QT prolongation
Concurrent use of IV methylene blue or certain linezolid regimens without close monitoring

efficacy_response.percentage_value: Many patients show initial benefit within 2 weeks
efficacy_response.comparison_data: Full antidepressant effects often require 4–6 weeks at a therapeutic dose.
efficacy_response.patient_text: Most people do not feel better immediately. It’s common to notice small changes in sleep, appetite, or energy after 1–2 weeks, with mood and anxiety improving more clearly over the next several weeks.

pharmacokinetics.onset: Initial mood effects in 1–2 weeks; full effect in 4–6 weeks
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: About 4 hours after a dose (range 1–6 hours)
pharmacokinetics.half_life: About 35 hours (longer in older adults and people with liver disease)
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Therapeutic drug levels maintained with once-daily dosing
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensively metabolized in the liver (mainly via CYP2C19 and CYP3A4, with some CYP2D6 involvement)
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Eliminated through both urine and stool (about 10% unchanged in urine)
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food has minimal impact; can be taken with or without food

sections.heading: What It’s Used For
sections.text: Citalopram is an SSRI antidepressant most commonly used to treat depression. It’s also frequently used off-label for several anxiety and mood-related conditions.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder}: Persistent low mood, loss of interest, and changes in sleep, appetite, and energy
{link:condition:generalized-anxiety-disorder:Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)}: Ongoing, hard-to-control worry about many areas of life
{link:condition:panic-disorder:Panic Disorder}: Repeated panic attacks and fear of having more attacks
{link:condition:social-anxiety-disorder:Social Anxiety Disorder}: Intense fear of being judged or embarrassed in social situations
{link:condition:obsessive-compulsive-disorder:Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)}: Repeated intrusive thoughts and compulsive behaviors
{link:condition:posttraumatic-stress-disorder:Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)}: Distressing memories, nightmares, and hyperarousal after trauma
off_label: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), using daily or cycle-based dosing
Premature ejaculation (helps delay ejaculation in some men)
Binge eating disorder (may reduce binge frequency in some cases)
Vasomotor symptoms of menopause (hot flashes) when hormones are not suitable
Agitation and aggression related to dementia, using lower doses and careful monitoring

sections.heading: What People Often Notice
sections.intro: Everyone is different, but many people describe a similar pattern when starting citalopram:

quotes: I didn’t feel happier yet, but my sleep and appetite started to normalize.
I felt a bit more restless and jittery at first, then it settled down.
Side effects showed up before the benefits—but they eased after a couple of weeks.
items.note: It’s common for side effects like nausea or sleep changes to appear early and improve with time.

quotes: I caught myself laughing again—I hadn’t done that in months.
The constant heavy feeling started to lift.
I still had bad days, but they didn’t knock me down as hard.
My mood is more stable and I bounce back faster from stress.
I don’t feel “high,” just more like myself again.
The anxiety is still there at times, but it’s turned way down.
The nausea was annoying at first, but it faded after a couple of weeks.
Sex is harder—my desire and ability to orgasm changed.
If I miss a few doses, I feel off—dizzy and irritable.
items.note: Sexual side effects and mild withdrawal symptoms with missed doses are common with SSRIs.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Citalopram does not work like a painkiller or anti-anxiety pill you feel within an hour. It builds up gradually and works over time.
key_points: 1–2 weeks: Many people notice small changes in sleep, appetite, or energy.
3–4 weeks: Mood and anxiety symptoms often start to improve more clearly.
4–6 weeks: Typical window to judge whether a dose is working.
≥6 weeks: Some conditions (like OCD or PTSD) may require 8–12 weeks at a stable dose.
Once-daily dosing: Because of its long half-life, most people take it once per day at the same time.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Citalopram carries a boxed warning for suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, teens, and young adults.
sections.black_box: Antidepressants, including citalopram, may increase the risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults, especially during the first few months of treatment or when the dose changes. All patients should be closely monitored for new or sudden changes in mood, behavior, thoughts of self-harm, or agitation. Citalopram is not approved for use in pediatric patients but may be used off-label when benefits outweigh risks.
other: Heart rhythm: Higher doses can affect the heart’s electrical system (QT prolongation), which can cause dangerous irregular heartbeats in at-risk people.
Dose limits: For most adults under 60, the usual maximum is 40 mg/day. For adults over 60, people with liver problems, or those taking certain interacting drugs, the maximum is 20 mg/day.
Serotonin syndrome: Combining citalopram with other serotonin-boosting drugs (certain antidepressants, migraine drugs, MAOIs, some supplements) can cause a rare but serious reaction.
Bleeding risk: May increase the risk of bruising and bleeding, especially when taken with blood thinners, aspirin, or NSAIDs.
Low sodium: Can cause low blood sodium, especially in older adults or people taking water pills (diuretics).
Mania switch: In people with bipolar disorder, antidepressants can trigger a manic or “too high” mood.
Withdrawal: Stopping suddenly can cause uncomfortable symptoms (dizziness, “brain zaps,” irritability, flu-like symptoms). Always taper with your prescriber.
patient_counseling: Tell your doctor right away if you have new or worsening depression, irritability, agitation, or any thoughts of self-harm—especially in the first few months or after dose changes.
Let your prescriber know about any history of heart problems, fainting, or family history of sudden cardiac death.
Bring a full list of your medications and supplements—many drugs can interact with citalopram.
Don’t stop citalopram suddenly, even if you feel better. Work with your prescriber on a slow taper.
If you feel unusually restless, overly energized, unable to sleep, or acting more impulsively than usual, contact your provider—this could be a mood switch.
Seek urgent care if you feel your heart racing or pounding, you faint, or you have severe dizziness.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most side effects are mild to moderate and improve with time. Serious side effects are uncommon but require urgent medical attention.
plain_language_list: Sexual side effects (lower desire, delayed orgasm, erection problems)

common.patient_note: Often worst in the first 1–2 weeks and improves if you take it with food or at night.
Some people feel more tired; others feel wired. Your prescriber may suggest taking it in the morning or evening depending on how it affects you.
Can lower desire or delay orgasm. This is a frequent reason people want to switch medications—talk openly with your prescriber if this happens.

common.incidence: Common, especially at the start or after dose increases
common.patient_note: Mild shaking or jitteriness usually settles down within a few weeks. If severe, contact your prescriber—your dose may need adjusting.
Night sweats or feeling clammy can occur. Dress in layers and stay hydrated; dose adjustment may help if severe.

serious: Fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat; fainting or severe dizziness (possible heart rhythm problem—seek emergency care).
Severe allergic reaction: swelling of the face, lips, or tongue; trouble breathing; hives (call 911).
Serotonin syndrome: high fever, confusion, stiff muscles, shivering, diarrhea, fast heart rate (emergency).
Severe confusion, strong headache, or unsteadiness (possible low sodium).
New or worsening suicidal thoughts or behavior—especially in younger patients.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Doses are individualized based on age, condition, and other medical issues. Your prescriber will usually start low and increase slowly to balance benefits and side effects.

adult.depression_initial: 20 mg once daily is a common starting dose. Some providers start at 10 mg once daily for sensitive or anxious patients.
adult.depression_titration: May increase by 10–20 mg at intervals of at least 1 week, depending on response and side effects.
adult.depression_max_under_60: 40 mg/day (do not exceed in most adults ≤60 years due to heart rhythm risk).
adult.depression_max_over_60: 20 mg/day (stricter limit because older adults have higher blood levels and higher QT risk).
adult.anxiety_disorders: Often start at 10 mg once daily and increase gradually in 10 mg steps every 1–2 weeks up to 20–40 mg/day (≤20 mg/day if >60 years).
adult.pmdd: 10–20 mg once daily, either all month or only during the 2 weeks before your period or from symptom onset until a few days into your period.
adult.premature_ejaculation: 20 mg once daily, with possible increase to 40 mg/day in adults ≤60 years if needed and tolerated.
adult.hepatic_impairment: Start at 10 mg once daily; do not exceed 20 mg/day.
adult.cyp2c19_poor_metabolizer_or_strong_inhib: Maximum 20 mg/day due to higher drug levels.
adult.renal_impairment_mild_to_moderate: Usually no change needed; monitor closely.
adult.renal_impairment_severe_or_dialysis: Often start at 10 mg once daily with cautious titration and heart rhythm monitoring.

sections.simple_explanation: For most adults, citalopram is taken once a day at the same time, with or without food. Higher doses are not always better—once you reach a therapeutic range (often 20–40 mg/day in younger adults), the focus is on staying consistent rather than continually increasing the dose.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Groups
sections.text: Citalopram can be used in pregnancy and breastfeeding when needed, but the decision is individualized. Older adults and people with medical conditions often need lower maximum doses and closer monitoring.
sections.pregnancy: Untreated depression and anxiety in pregnancy can harm both parent and baby. Citalopram has been studied in pregnancy and is not clearly linked to a major increase in overall birth defects, but late-pregnancy use may cause temporary withdrawal-like symptoms or breathing issues in newborns. Decisions should be made with your obstetric and mental health providers based on your history and severity of symptoms.
sections.lactation: Citalopram passes into breast milk in small amounts. Most breastfed infants do well, but some may be extra sleepy, irritable, or feed poorly. If you take citalopram while breastfeeding, your baby’s pediatrician can monitor weight gain, feeding, and behavior.
sections.pediatrics: Citalopram is not FDA-approved for children or teens but may be used off-label for depression or anxiety when other options are not suitable. Lower starting doses and slow titration are important. Closely monitor for suicidal thoughts, agitation, or unusual behavior changes.
sections.geriatrics: Adults 60 and older generally should not exceed 20 mg/day due to higher blood levels and increased risk of heart rhythm changes. Older adults are also more prone to low sodium, falls, and bleeding, so closer monitoring is needed.
sections.hepatic: People with liver disease clear the drug more slowly. They usually need lower maximum doses (≤20 mg/day) and slow titration.
sections.renal: Mild to moderate kidney disease usually does not require dose changes, but severe kidney disease or dialysis may require a lower starting dose and careful monitoring of side effects and heart rhythm.

sections.heading: Drug and Supplement Interactions
sections.intro: Citalopram interacts with many medications. Always check with your prescriber or pharmacist before adding new prescriptions or over-the-counter products.

items.with: Other antidepressants, MAOIs, certain migraine medications, St. John’s wort, or other serotonin-boosting drugs
items.risk: Higher risk of serotonin syndrome (agitation, fever, stiff muscles, confusion).
items.action: Avoid risky combinations when possible. If used together under medical supervision, monitor closely for symptoms.

items.with: Medications that affect heart rhythm (other QT-prolonging drugs)
items.risk: Greater chance of dangerous heart rhythm changes.
items.action: Your prescriber may choose another antidepressant or check an EKG and blood electrolytes before and during treatment.

items.with: Blood thinners (warfarin), antiplatelet drugs (aspirin, clopidogrel), NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen)
items.risk: Increased tendency to bruise or bleed, including in the stomach or intestines.
items.action: Use cautiously and watch for black stools, vomiting blood, or unusual bruising.

items.with: Diuretics (water pills) and other medications that lower sodium
items.risk: Higher risk of low sodium levels, which can cause confusion, headache, or unsteadiness.
items.action: Your provider may monitor your blood sodium, especially early in treatment and after dose changes.

items.with: Strong CYP2C19 inhibitors (for example, some heartburn medications) or known CYP2C19 poor metabolizer status
items.risk: Higher blood levels of citalopram, increasing side effect and QT risk.
items.action: Maximum dose is usually reduced to 20 mg/day; EKG monitoring may be considered.

sections.heading: Stopping Citalopram Safely
sections.text: Do not stop citalopram suddenly unless your doctor tells you to. A slow, planned taper reduces the chance of withdrawal symptoms and helps detect symptom relapse early.
key_points: Typical tapers reduce the dose gradually over at least 2–4 weeks after long-term use, sometimes longer.
Stopping too quickly can cause dizziness, “electric shock” sensations in the head, nausea, irritability, and flu-like symptoms.
If withdrawal symptoms are severe, your prescriber may briefly increase the dose again and then taper more slowly.
People who have been on antidepressants for many months or years may benefit from very gradual tapers over several months.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Citalopram is available in generic and brand forms. All forms are designed for once-daily use.
items: Tablets: Common strengths include 10 mg, 20 mg, and 40 mg.
Oral solution: Liquid citalopram for people who have trouble swallowing pills.
Capsules (some markets): May be available in specific strengths (for example, 30 mg).

sections.heading: How It Works in the Brain
sections.text: Citalopram is an SSRI—it blocks the reuptake (recycling) of serotonin in the brain, which increases serotonin levels between nerve cells. Over time, this helps reset overactive or underactive brain circuits involved in mood, anxiety, and stress. It does not create artificial happiness; instead, it supports your brain’s ability to regulate emotions more normally.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment
sections.text: Citalopram is considered one of several first-line SSRI options for depression and many anxiety disorders. It is often chosen when a once-daily, generally well-tolerated antidepressant is desired. However, because higher doses can affect heart rhythm, some clinicians prefer other SSRIs for people who may need very high doses or who already have heart rhythm risk factors.

sections.heading: What Clinicians Monitor
items: Mood and anxiety symptoms: Improvement in core symptoms and overall functioning.
Suicidal thoughts or behavior: Especially in the first 1–2 months and after any dose change.
Heart rhythm: EKG in patients with heart disease, on interacting drugs, or needing higher doses.
Electrolytes: Blood potassium and magnesium in people at risk for low levels.
Sodium levels: Particularly in older adults or those on diuretics.
Side effects: Sexual changes, sleep issues, GI symptoms, and any signs of serotonin syndrome.
Weight and appetite: Especially in children, teens, and older adults.
Bleeding signs: Easy bruising, nosebleeds, or black/tarry stools in patients on blood thinners or NSAIDs.

seo.title: Citalopram (Celexa): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects & Safety
seo.description: Citalopram (Celexa) for depression and anxiety: how it works, typical doses, how long it takes to work, common side effects, heart rhythm and suicide risk warnings, pregnancy/breastfeeding, and safe tapering.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and aligned with current FDA prescribing information, major clinical practice guidelines, and recent peer-reviewed literature on SSRI use, cardiac safety, and reproductive considerations.

faqs.a: Citalopram (Celexa) is an SSRI antidepressant used to treat major depressive disorder in adults. Doctors also prescribe it off-label for several anxiety-related conditions, including generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, OCD, PTSD, PMDD, and sometimes for hot flashes or premature ejaculation.

faqs.q: How long does it take for citalopram to work?
faqs.a: You usually won’t feel better right away. Many people notice small improvements in sleep, energy, or appetite after 1–2 weeks, with mood and anxiety improving more clearly over the next 2–4 weeks. It often takes 4–6 weeks at a stable dose to judge how well it’s working.

faqs.q: What is the usual dose of citalopram?
faqs.a: A common starting dose for adults is 20 mg once daily, although some people start at 10 mg to reduce early side effects. For most adults under 60, the usual maximum is 40 mg/day. For adults 60 and older or those with liver problems, the maximum is 20 mg/day because of heart rhythm risk.

faqs.q: Why can’t I go above 40 mg of citalopram?
faqs.a: Doses above 40 mg/day increase the risk of changes in the heart’s electrical rhythm (QT prolongation), which can lead to dangerous irregular heartbeats in some people. For adults 60 and older or those with liver disease or certain drug interactions, the maximum recommended dose is 20 mg/day for the same reason.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects of citalopram?
faqs.a: Common side effects include nausea, dry mouth, tiredness or trouble sleeping, sweating, tremor, headache, and sexual side effects such as lower desire or delayed orgasm. These are often mild to moderate and can improve over time. If side effects are bothersome or don’t go away, talk with your prescriber about options.

At higher doses or in people with certain risk factors, citalopram can lengthen the heart’s electrical recovery time (QT interval), which in rare cases can trigger dangerous heart rhythms. This is why there are strict dose limits and why some patients need an EKG and electrolyte checks.

Citalopram is not addictive in the way drugs of abuse are, and it is not a controlled substance. However, your brain gets used to having it on board, so stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms (dizziness, irritability, “brain zaps,” flu-like feelings). That’s why it should be tapered slowly with your prescriber.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking citalopram?
faqs.a: Moderate alcohol is not strictly banned, but combining alcohol with citalopram can worsen drowsiness, coordination problems, and depression or anxiety. Many clinicians recommend limiting or avoiding alcohol, especially when you’re just starting the medication or if you have a history of substance use or mood instability.

faqs.q: Is citalopram safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Citalopram has been fairly well studied in pregnancy and breastfeeding. It may be appropriate when untreated depression or anxiety would pose greater risk than the medication. Some newborns exposed late in pregnancy may have temporary withdrawal-like symptoms. The decision is individualized—always discuss with your obstetric and mental health providers.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss a dose of citalopram?
faqs.a: If you forget a dose and remember the same day, take it as soon as you remember. If it’s almost time for your next dose, skip the missed one and just take your regular dose—don’t double up. Missing doses occasionally may cause you to feel more down or experience mild withdrawal symptoms, so try to take it at the same time every day.

faqs.q: How do I stop taking citalopram safely?
faqs.a: Never stop abruptly on your own. Work with your prescriber to create a taper plan—usually lowering the dose gradually over several weeks or longer, depending on how long you’ve been on it and at what dose. If you develop significant withdrawal symptoms during a taper, your dose may be briefly increased and then reduced more slowly.
